unit.title: Prepare vegetables, fruits, eggs and farinaceous dishes

essays.stem: Explain how to prepare and cook ackee safely for ackee and saltfish.
essays.modelAnswer: Ackee is safe only when it is ripe. I use only ackee from pods that have opened naturally on the tree and show the yellow flesh and black seeds. Unripe or forced-open ackee has a natural poison that can make people very ill, so I never use it. I take the yellow flesh out of the pod and remove every black seed and the pink-red membrane inside, and throw these away with the pods. I wash the ackee in cold water. I boil it gently in salted water for a few minutes until it is just tender, then drain it and throw the water away. I handle it gently so it does not break up. I fold it into the cooked saltfish with onion, sweet pepper, tomato, thyme, scallion and Scotch bonnet pepper, and heat it through without stirring too much. If I use canned ackee, I check the can is not dented or swollen and that it comes from an approved supplier. I serve it hot with fried dumplings, boiled green banana or breadfruit.
markingPoints: Use only ripe ackee from pods that opened naturally; never unripe
Explains that unripe ackee is poisonous
Remove all seeds and the pink-red membrane, and wash the ackee
Boil until just tender, drain and throw away the water; handle gently
Combine with saltfish and seasoning; canned ackee checked (sound can, approved supplier)

essays.stem: Describe how to receive and store different kinds of vegetables and fruit so that they stay fresh.
essays.modelAnswer: When vegetables and fruit arrive, I check them. They should be firm, with a bright colour and no bruises, mould, soft spots, insects or wilting. I check the amounts against the order, and I tell the supervisor about anything that is not right. Then I store each kind in the right place. Ground provisions such as yam, sweet potato, coco and Irish potato go in a cool, dark, dry and airy place, off the floor, so they do not rot, sprout or turn green. Onions and garlic go in a dry, airy place too. Leafy vegetables such as lettuce, callaloo and pak choi go in the fridge, in covered containers, so they do not wilt. Soft fruit, cut fruit and salad items also go in the fridge. Some fruit, such as bananas and unripe mangoes and pawpaw, are left out of the fridge to ripen. I keep raw vegetables with soil on them away from ready-to-eat food. I label and date the stock and use the oldest first (first in, first out), and I check stored produce every day and remove anything going bad.
markingPoints: Checks quality on delivery (firm, bright, no bruises or mould) and the amounts; reports problems
Ground provisions and onions in a cool, dark, dry, airy place off the floor
Leafy vegetables, soft and cut fruit in the fridge, covered
Some fruit ripened out of the fridge; soil-covered produce kept away from ready-to-eat food
Label, date, first in first out, and daily checks

essays.stem: Explain how to prepare and cook green vegetables, such as callaloo or string beans, so that they keep their colour, flavour and vitamins.
essays.modelAnswer: Green vegetables lose colour and vitamins if they are cut too early, soaked, or cooked too long. I wash them well in cold water to remove soil and insects, but I do not leave them soaking. For callaloo, I strip the tough skin from the stems and chop the leaves and tender stems. For string beans, I top and tail them and cut them to an even size so they cook evenly. I prepare them close to cooking time. I cook them quickly. Callaloo is steamed in a covered pot with a little water, butter or oil, onion, garlic, tomato and thyme, for only a few minutes until it is just tender. String beans can be boiled in a small amount of boiling salted water, without a lid, or steamed, until just tender, then served at once, or blanched and refreshed in iced water and reheated later. I never add bicarbonate of soda, because it destroys vitamins. I cook small batches close to service so they stay bright green and do not go dull and soft.
markingPoints: Wash well but do not soak; prepare close to cooking
Trim and cut evenly (strip callaloo stems, top and tail beans)
Cook quickly, just until tender, by steaming or in a little boiling water
Blanch and refresh if cooking ahead; no bicarbonate of soda
Cook small batches close to service to keep colour and vitamins

essays.stem: Describe how to prepare and boil ground provisions (such as yam, sweet potato and green banana) and boiled dumplings for service.
essays.modelAnswer: I wash the provisions to remove soil. Green bananas stain the hands, so I wear gloves or oil my hands, cut off the ends, slit the skin along its length, and either boil them in the skin or peel them first. I peel the yam and sweet potato with a knife or peeler, cutting away from my body, and cut them into even pieces so they cook at the same time. I keep the peeled yam in cold water for a short time so it does not darken. For the dumplings, I mix flour and a pinch of salt with cold water and knead it into a smooth, firm dough. I pinch off pieces, roll them into balls and flatten them a little. I put the provisions in a pot of boiling salted water, with the harder yam first, and add the dumplings. I boil them until a knife goes in easily and the dumplings float and are firm, which takes about 15 to 25 minutes. I drain them and serve them hot, or keep them hot at about 63 °C or above, with ackee and saltfish or a stew.
markingPoints: Wash; green bananas trimmed, slit and peeled (or boiled in skin) with gloves or oiled hands
Peel safely and cut into even pieces
Dumplings: flour, salt and water kneaded into a firm dough and shaped
Boil in salted water until tender; dumplings float and are firm
Drain and serve hot, or hot-hold at about 63 °C or above

essays.stem: Describe how to poach an egg, and how to make a callaloo omelette.
essays.modelAnswer: To poach an egg, I use a fresh egg, because the white holds together better. I heat a wide pan of water with a little vinegar until it is just simmering, with small bubbles. I crack the egg into a small cup, then slide it gently into the water. I cook it for about 3 to 4 minutes, until the white is set and the yolk is still soft, or longer if the guest wants it firm. I lift it out with a slotted spoon, drain it on kitchen paper and trim any ragged edges. For a callaloo omelette, I first steam the callaloo with onion and tomato and keep it hot. I crack 2 or 3 eggs into a bowl, check for shell, add a little salt and pepper, and beat them well with a fork. I heat a little butter or oil in an omelette pan until it is hot. I pour in the eggs and stir quickly with a fork, shaking the pan, until they are lightly set. I put the callaloo in the middle, fold the omelette over and roll it onto a warm plate. I serve both straight away.
markingPoints: Poached egg: fresh egg, water just simmering with a little vinegar
Slide the egg in from a cup; cook about 3–4 minutes until the white is set; drain and trim
Omelette: eggs cracked into a bowl, checked, seasoned and beaten
Cooked quickly in a hot buttered pan, stirred until lightly set
Callaloo filling added, folded and served at once on a warm plate

essays.stem: Explain how to receive, store and handle eggs safely in a kitchen.
essays.modelAnswer: Eggs can carry Salmonella bacteria on the shell and sometimes inside, so they must be handled with care. When eggs arrive, I check that the shells are clean and not cracked, and that the boxes are dated. I do not accept cracked or very dirty eggs. I store eggs in the fridge, in their boxes, away from strong-smelling foods and away from ready-to-eat food, and I use the oldest first (first in, first out). I do not wash eggs before storing them, unless the Centre's plan says so. I crack eggs into a small bowl one at a time, so a bad egg or a piece of shell can be removed. I wash my hands after handling raw eggs and shells. For dishes that are not cooked, such as fresh mayonnaise, I use pasteurised eggs. Egg dishes for young children, pregnant guests and older people are cooked until the white and yolk are set. Cooked egg dishes are served at once or kept hot at about 63 °C or above, or chilled quickly, and leftovers are covered, labelled and dated.
markingPoints: Explains the Salmonella risk
Checks eggs on delivery: clean, not cracked, dated
Stores in the fridge away from strong smells; first in, first out
Cracks eggs into a separate bowl; washes hands after handling raw eggs
Pasteurised eggs for uncooked dishes; fully cooked for vulnerable guests; correct holding

essays.stem: Describe how to cook Jamaican rice and peas, starting from dried red kidney beans.
essays.modelAnswer: The night before, I pick over the dried kidney beans to remove stones, wash them and soak them in cold water. Next day, I throw away the soaking water and put the beans in a pot with fresh water. I boil them hard for at least the first part of the cooking, because raw kidney beans contain a natural toxin that boiling destroys. Then I simmer them until they are soft but not broken, which can take an hour or more, or less in a pressure cooker used as the maker says. I add coconut milk, crushed garlic, a sprig of thyme, scallion, pimento berries, salt and a whole Scotch bonnet pepper, which must not burst. I measure the liquid for the amount of rice. I wash the rice, add it and bring it to the boil, then cover the pot and turn the heat low so the rice takes in all the liquid. When the rice is tender and dry, I remove the pepper and thyme stalk and fluff the rice with a fork. I serve it hot, or cool any extra quickly and store it in the fridge.
markingPoints: Pick over, wash and soak the beans overnight; throw away the soaking water
Boil hard in fresh water, then simmer until soft (safety reason given)
Add coconut milk and seasonings (garlic, thyme, scallion, pimento, whole Scotch bonnet, salt)
Measure liquid, add washed rice, cover and cook on a low heat until the liquid is absorbed
Fluff and serve hot; cool leftovers quickly and refrigerate

essays.stem: Describe how to cook dried pasta correctly, and how to hold or store it if it is not served at once.
essays.modelAnswer: I check the cooking time on the packet. I bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil, using about 1 litre of water for each 100 g of pasta, and add salt. I add the pasta all at once and stir it straight away, so the pieces do not stick together. I keep the water boiling and stir now and then. I start tasting a piece a minute or two before the packet time. The pasta is ready when it is al dente, which means cooked but still firm to the bite. I drain it in a colander in the sink, pouring away from my body to avoid steam burns. If I am serving it at once, I toss it with the sauce. If it is for later, I rinse it under cold water to stop the cooking, drain it well, toss it in a little oil so it does not stick, cool it quickly, and store it covered, labelled and dated in the fridge at 5 °C or below. To reheat, I drop it into boiling water for a short time, or heat it in the sauce until it is piping hot.
markingPoints: Plenty of boiling salted water (about 1 litre per 100 g)
Add pasta and stir straight away and now and then so it does not stick
Taste before the packet time; cook until al dente
Drain safely, pouring away from the body
If not served at once: cool quickly, oil lightly, cover, label and refrigerate; reheat until piping hot

essays.stem: Describe how to prepare a Jamaican fruit platter so that the fruit is safe and looks fresh.
essays.modelAnswer: I choose ripe, firm fruit in season, such as pineapple, mango, pawpaw, watermelon, banana and June plum, and check that it has no mould or bruises. I wash my hands and wash all the fruit, even the fruit I will peel, because a knife can carry dirt from the skin into the flesh. I use a clean board kept for fruit and salad (green in the usual colour code) and a sharp knife. I cut off the top and base of the pineapple, cut off the skin, remove the eyes and core, and slice it. I peel the mango and pawpaw, take out the seeds, and cut them into even slices or wedges. I cut fruit that turns brown, such as banana, last, and squeeze a little lime juice over it. I arrange the fruit on a chilled platter in neat rows or groups of colour, with a garnish such as mint. I cover the platter and keep it in the fridge at 5 °C or below until service, and I do not leave it out for longer than the Centre's food safety plan allows.
markingPoints: Choose ripe, sound fruit; wash hands and wash all fruit before cutting
Clean fruit board and sharp knife
Correct preparation: peel, remove seeds, cores and eyes; even pieces
Lime juice on fruit that browns; neat, colourful arrangement
Covered and chilled at 5 °C or below until service; time out limited

essays.topic: Food safety: rice and starchy foods
essays.stem: Explain how to cool, store and reheat cooked rice and other starchy foods safely.
essays.modelAnswer: Cooked rice, pasta and other starchy foods can carry bacteria that survive cooking and make poisons if the food is left warm, so they must not stay in the danger zone, between 5 °C and 63 °C. If rice is not served at once, I cool it quickly. I spread it in a thin layer on a clean, shallow tray and leave it in a cool place for a short time, then cover it and put it in the fridge as soon as it has cooled, within the time the Centre's food safety plan gives. I label it with the name and the date, store it at 5 °C or below, and use it within the time the plan allows. I never leave rice on the counter or in a warm pot for hours. To reheat, I heat only what I need until it is steaming hot all the way through, about 74 °C at the core, checked with a clean probe. I reheat it once only. Rice or pasta kept hot for service is held at about 63 °C or above. Anything left over after reheating is thrown away.
markingPoints: Explains why rice is a risk if left warm
Cool quickly in a thin layer in a shallow tray, then refrigerate
Cover, label and date; store at 5 °C or below; use in the allowed time
Reheat until steaming hot (about 74 °C core), once only
Hot-hold at about 63 °C or above; throw away leftovers after reheating

practical1.title: Jamaican vegetable plate and tropical fruit platter
practical1.brief: As a group, prepare a vegetable plate for 4 guests and a fruit platter for 8. The plate has steamed callaloo, roasted breadfruit (or roasted pumpkin and sweet potato if breadfruit is not in season), fried ripe plantain, and boiled green banana. Each member takes charge of one item and helps with the others: washing and preparing the vegetables, cutting them to an even size, cooking them by the right method, and keeping them hot. For the fruit platter, every member washes, peels and cuts at least one kind of fruit (such as pineapple, mango, pawpaw, watermelon), and the group arranges the platter and keeps it covered in the fridge until the assessor checks it. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the plates and platter are done and the area is clean.
materials: 1 bundle of callaloo, onion, tomato, garlic, thyme, butter or oil
1 breadfruit, or pumpkin and sweet potato
A selection of local fruit: pineapple, mango, pawpaw, watermelon, limes
Cook's knives, paring knives, peelers, boards in the Centre's colour code
Steamer or pot with lid, frying pan, roasting tray, oven
Platter, plates, cling film, labels, probe thermometer
Disposable gloves, detergent, food-safe sanitiser, clean cloths
photos: All the vegetables and fruit washed and laid out, with each member's job shown
The callaloo stripped and chopped, and the plantain and bananas peeled and cut
The breadfruit or pumpkin roasting, and the callaloo steaming
The fried plantain draining on kitchen paper
The fruit cut into even pieces on the fruit board
The finished fruit platter, covered and labelled in the fridge
checklist: Washed hands and washed all produce before peeling and cutting
Used the right board and a sharp knife, cutting away from the body and with a safe grip
Cut the vegetables and fruit into neat, even pieces
Cooked each vegetable by a suitable method until just tender, keeping the colour
Fried the plantain safely, laying it into the oil away from the body
Used lime juice on fruit that browns, and kept the platter covered and chilled
Plated neatly and served hot food hot, on warm plates
Cleaned and sanitised the work area and equipment, and sorted the waste
safety: Wear gloves or oil your hands when peeling green bananas, and grip them firmly
Carry knives point down, and never try to catch a falling knife
Use dry oven cloths for hot trays and turn pan handles inwards
Never leave hot oil unattended; keep a fire blanket near
Wipe up spills and peelings from the floor straight away

practical2.title: Rice and peas, boiled dumplings, macaroni pie and egg dishes
practical2.brief: As a group, cook rice and peas and boiled dumplings for 6 portions, and a macaroni pie for 6, and each member cooks two egg dishes to order. Use red kidney beans that the Centre soaked overnight (with the soaking water thrown away), or tinned red peas. Two members make the rice and peas, boiling the beans hard first, then adding coconut milk, seasoning and rice. Two members make the dumpling dough, shape and boil the dumplings. The others boil the macaroni until just tender, make the cheese sauce and bake the pie. While these cook, each member, in turn, poaches one egg and makes one omelette (plain or with callaloo) for the assessor. Plate one full serving of rice and peas, dumplings and macaroni pie, and each member's egg dishes. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the plates are done and the area is clean.
materials: Red kidney beans (soaked overnight) or tinned red peas, rice, coconut milk
Garlic, thyme, scallion, pimento berries, Scotch bonnet pepper, salt
Macaroni, butter, flour, milk, cheese, eggs for the pie
2 eggs and some callaloo for each member
Pots with lids, omelette pan, slotted spoon, baking dish, oven
Measuring jugs and scales, probe thermometer, plates
photos: The ingredients weighed and measured for each dish
The beans boiling hard in fresh water, then the rice and peas cooking
The dumpling dough kneaded, and the shaped dumplings
The boiled macaroni draining, and the pie ready for the oven
Each member's poached egg on the plate
Each member's omelette on the plate
The finished plate of rice and peas, dumplings and macaroni pie, and the clean work area
checklist: Weighed and measured ingredients as the recipe says
Boiled the soaked beans hard in fresh water before simmering
Cooked the rice and peas until the liquid was absorbed and the rice tender, not burnt
Made a smooth, firm dumpling dough and boiled the dumplings until cooked through
Cooked the macaroni al dente, and baked the pie until golden and hot all through
